nameStory: The word "beaver" comes from the Old English "beofor," which traces back to ancient words meaning "brown." These industrious rodents earned their reputation as nature's engineers long before humans had a name for them, but the "American" part distinguishes our North American species from their Eurasian cousins across the pond.
description: American beavers are North America's largest rodents, built like living bulldozers with flat, scaly tails and webbed hind feet. Adults can weigh 35-60 pounds and measure up to 4 feet long including their distinctive paddle-shaped tail. Their thick, waterproof fur ranges from golden brown to dark chocolate, and their large orange front teeth never stop growing. These semi-aquatic mammals are famous for building dams, lodges, and completely reshaping waterways with their engineering skills.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, barrel-shaped body about the size of a medium dog, with a distinctive flat, leathery tail that feels like a tennis racket and sounds like a gunshot when slapped on water

idTips.label: Teeth & Head
idTips.description: Large, bright orange front teeth (incisors) visible even when mouth is closed, small rounded ears that can close underwater, dark beady eyes positioned high on the head

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, glossy coat that feels oily to the touch and ranges from rich golden-brown to dark chocolate; water beads right off it like a raincoat

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Large webbed hind prints (5-7 inches) with five toes, smaller front paws with long claws, often accompanied by a drag mark from the heavy tail

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Cone-shaped tree stumps with distinctive chisel marks from those orange teeth, plus stick-and-mud dams, dome-shaped lodges, and wood chips that smell fresh and piney

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Most active at dawn and dusk, swimming with just head visible above water, diving with a loud tail slap when startled, methodically gnawing through trees

habitat: Beavers need slow-moving or still water near deciduous trees, so look for them along streams, ponds, marshes, and river backwaters throughout New England's forests. They prefer areas with aspen, birch, willow, and poplar trees within 150 feet of water. You'll often find them in areas they've modified themselves, creating ponds by damming small streams in valleys and wetland edges.

seasonality.spring: Most active as ice melts and they repair winter damage to dams and lodges. Fresh wood chips and newly chewed stumps appear as they take advantage of rising sap in trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with lots of swimming, dam building, and tree cutting. Look for fresh mud and sticks added to dams, and listen for tail slaps on calm evenings.
seasonality.fall: Busy storing branches underwater near their lodges for winter food. You'll see the most tree-cutting activity and fresh wood chips as they prepare for cold months.
seasonality.winter: Less visible but still active under ice, living off stored branches. Look for maintained holes in ice near lodges and continued fresh signs during warm spells.

funFact: A beaver's front teeth are self-sharpening - the back side wears away faster than the front, maintaining a perfect chisel edge that can chew through a 4-inch tree in just 15 minutes!
confusionNotes: Often confused with muskrats, but beavers are much larger (muskrats are house cat-sized) and have flat tails instead of skinny rat-like tails. Remember: "Flat tail = beaver, rat tail = muskrat." River otters are sleeker and more playful, with long muscular tails rather than paddle-shaped ones.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse American beavers with "mountain beavers" - despite the name, mountain beavers are completely unrelated rodents that don't even build dams! The American beaver is also called the Canadian beaver, reflecting their importance as a national symbol of Canada, though they're equally at home throughout New England.
compareHints: American beavers are the only beaver species in New England, but they're quite different from their closest living relatives, the Eurasian beavers found in Europe and Asia. While very similar in appearance and behavior, Eurasian beavers are slightly smaller and have narrower tails and skulls. Within the rodent family, beavers are unique in their large size and aquatic engineering lifestyle.
